Heiligenkreuz
HY-lee-gen-kroyts
n. (the Lower Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1133, inhabited without a break since, where the divine office has been sung for nearly nine centuries)
German Heiligenkreuz, holy cross, from the relic given by Duke Leopold V.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Heiligenkreuz in the Vienna woods was founded in 1133 by Leopold III of Babenberg and settled from Morimond, and it takes its name from a relic of the cross brought back by Leopold V. It is the oldest continuously inhabited Cistercian house in the world: the community has never been dispersed, not by Joseph II's suppressions, not by the Turks who reached its walls twice, not by the Nazi government that seized the buildings in 1940, and the seven hours of the divine office have been sung in its choir for nearly nine centuries. The chapter house holds the Babenberg tombs. The dictionary records Heiligenkreuz not for its relic, which belongs with the corruptions, but for that unbroken recitation, because continuance in prayer is commanded in terms that admit no interval, “Pray without ceasing” (1Th 5:17). The apostolic word for the practice is a verb of persistence with thanksgiving attached, “Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2). The posture is a watchman's through a long night, “My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning” (Psa 130:6), and the access that makes such persistence reasonable is open to every believer and needs no choir, “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the office in this sense as a formulary of devotion; a choir as the part of a church where the singers are placed; matins as morning worship; vigils as devotional watching; and to intercede as to plead in favor of another.

expand to see more

OFFICE, n. A formulary of devotion; the daily service of the breviary; also, duty, employment.

CHOIR, n. A band or collection of singers; also, the part of a church appropriated to the singers.

MATINS, n. Morning worship or service; morning prayers or songs.

VIGIL, n. Watch; devotional watching; the eve or day preceding a church festival.

BREVIARY, n. A book containing the daily service of the Roman Catholic or Greek church.

Key Scripture

1Th 5:17 — "Pray without ceasing."

Col 4:2 — "Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving;"

Psa 130:6 — "My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning."

Heb 4:16 — "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."

Modern Corruption

The oldest continuously inhabited Cistercian house in the world, founded 1133, where the office has been sung without a break.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that persistence in prayer is commanded and that nine centuries of it is therefore not excessive. Heiligenkreuz has never missed the hours, and the apostolic instruction is given without a stated limit, “Pray without ceasing” (1Th 5:17).

The live temptation is the one Heiligenkreuz's name carries: the house was endowed around a fragment of wood, and a relic proposes to supply an access already granted. Scripture gives the practice its proper companion, “and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2), its proper posture, “more than they that watch for the morning” (Psa 130:6), and its proper ground, which is a throne approached directly and boldly, “that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek adialeiptos (G0089), unceasingly; Greek proskartereo (G4342), to continue steadfastly; Hebrew qavah (H6960), to wait for; Greek parrhesia (G3954), boldness of access.

expand to see more

Greek adialeiptos (G0089) — without intermission, unceasingly; “Pray without ceasing”, 1 Thessalonians 5:17.

Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to continue steadfastly, to persevere in; “Continue in prayer”, Colossians 4:2.

Greek eucharistia (G2169) — thanksgiving, gratitude; “and watch in the same with thanksgiving”, Colossians 4:2.

Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look eagerly for; “My soul waiteth for the Lord”, Psalm 130:6.

Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of access; “come boldly unto the throne of grace”, Hebrews 4:16.

Usage

"“Pray without ceasing” (1Th 5:17) — a command with no stated interval."

"“Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2) — persistence with its companion."

"“come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16) — the access a relic cannot improve."
